subsubtopic: JUDGMENT OF DOMINION RAILWAY COMMISSION
speechtext:
I should like to ask the Minister of Justice a question based on an order or judgment of a majority of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, effective March I, granting a substantial increase of rates to the Bell Telephone Company. An appeal is being taken on questions of both law and fact to the Supreme court and Governor General in Council. As the case is still sub judice will the Minister of Justice, as Attorney General of Canada, or the government under the Railway Act, grant a stay for thirty days of this order, or request the commissioners so to do before these new schedules of rates are sanctioned, especially as one of the board in a dissenting judgment holds that both the law and the facts were against the company's contention?
This would be a reasonable application of the doctrine of sub judice. Section 56 of the Railway Act defines the powers of the Governor General in Council as follows:
The governor in council may at any time, in his discretion, either upon petition of any party, person or company interested, or of his own motion, and without any petition or application. vary or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the boards, whether such order or decision is made inter partes or otherwise, and whether such regulation is general or limited

in its scope and application; and any order which the governor in council may make with respect thereto shall be binding upon the board and upon all parties.
I would suggest that the minister might answer this to-morrow.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. C. HOCKEN (Toronto West Centre):
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having regard to the pledges of the government and to the large support that the government gets from the free trade element in this House, I presume that we on this side who believe in reasonable protection for the industries of the country ought to feel more or less satisfied that this particular budget does not further reduce tariff duties. It will be a disappointment to my hon. friend from Rosetown (Mr. Evans), who predicted last session that -there would probably be a reduction in the duty on boots and shoes. But boots and shoes is a very tender spot in the tariff with many hon. gentlemen opposite. The rosy picture which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) paints of present conditions in Canada are not at all in accordance with the facts. I am prepared to admit that there is some slight improvement in trade, but it is more a hopeful spirit than any actual advance in conditions of trade and industry throughout the country. I judge, from what we have read from the general managers of our banks, that a concerted effort is being made by them, which perhaps is very laudable, to cultivate a spirit of optimism in the country, and in that desire they have gone much further than the facts would warrant. I do not think any person who has a knowledge of the industrial situation to-day can claim that this country enjoys that abounding prosperity referred to by the minister. The only class that is fully employed in Canada to-day is the farming community; and of course the farmer has always a job. But if you get into general industry you find a great many factories working half time, a great many closed down, and a general state of anxiety on the part of those who have the management of these enterprises under their charge.
I am not surprised to learn that the unemployment index is better now than it was last year. 'This is due, not to a larger number in employment, but to the fact that there are fewer people to be employed. When our people are leaving the country at the rate of 100.000 a year, there are inevitably fewer unemployed left at home. And that is exactly the situation so far as general industry is concerned. There may be an industry here or there enjoying special favours, like the implement industry which is doing very well, but if you take the whole range of industrial activities throughout the country you will find that the conditions are not at all such as are described by the Minister of Finance.

I fancy my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) will not expect the members of this party to have any particular sympathy with his amendment. Speaking for myself, at any rate, I must say I have no sympathy for it. It comprises two things: first, a demand for lower duties, and secondly, a protest against the reduction in the income tax. Now, we are not going to get any lower duties this year, and I think the explanation given by the government, as indicated by my hon. friend from South Huron (Mr. McMillan) yesterday, is quite reasonable. He points out that the ministers have been so busy that they have been unable to prepare a budget providing for lower duties. That is a fair explanation; it is one that any free trader on the other side of the House may find it easy to accept. There appear, however, to be one or two over there who do not accept it. although the hon. member for South Huron, at least, does. And, as I say, it appeals to me as a reasonable explanation. The protest against the reduction in the income tax, embodied in the amendment, comes properly from a section of the country that does not pay any income tax worth speaking about. Take the province of Saskatchewan for example : the total payments of income tax there work out at an insignificant fraction over one dollar per head of the population. If you take Ontario, on the other hand, you will find the per capita income tax given at $8.66. So that hon. members from the prairies who pay no income tax-

Let me now refer for a moment or two to certain statements made by the hon. mem-
The Budget-Mr. Hocken

ber for South Huron yesterday. The burden of his speech was that agriculture in Canada does not receive from government the consideration that it deserves. I should like to know wherein agriculture is denied consideration by this government or by the government of any province of the Dominion. I agree with the hon. member that it is the basic industry, and at the present day the largest in Canada. But there is no industry in this country which receives so much consideration from eveiy form of government as does agriculture. In the first place there are special freight rates for the western agriculturist- the lowest freight rates in the world, rates which the railways tell us are not adequate to meet the cost of transportation. If that is the case, that low rate must be made up by the central provinces and by the taxpayers generally. Agriculture in the west enjoys, therefore, a special subsidy in the low freight rates which it gets and which the taxpayers of Canada at large must pay.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: What authority has the hon. member for the statement that the railways have declared the rates unequal to the cost?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows
very well that it is by an act of this House that the west gets the special freight rates which it enjoys to-day; and he knows very welll that those rates wmuld be higher if they were placed on a parity with the freight rates throughout Canada. There is no doubt about that. These freight rates are in effect a subsidy, a bounty to the grain growers. But it is not only in that respect that agriculture is considered. Travel throughout the country and you will find in every province experimental farms conducted for the benefit of the agricultural industry; a central farm adjoining this city and farms in every province in the Dominion. These institutions are comparable with the laboratories of great industries. An industry that wants to improve its methods, to find more efficient plans to carry on, has to engage experts at large salaries and maintain large staffs in order to improve and reduce the cost of its product.
I am not objecting to' that. That is an expense which all other industries have to meet, but which in the case of agriculture is met by the Dominion government and all -the provincial governments. Surely that is a consideration that should be taken into account. Not only experimental farms but agricultural colleges exist everywhere for the special training of agriculturists and for improving their plans.
(Mr. Hanson.]

I think agriculture depends upon other industries as much as other industries depend upon agriculture, and if my hon. friend will allow me I shall have a word to say about that later.
My hon. friend enlarged upon the decreasing agricultural population particularly in the United States. I do not know how much he has read on the subject; but I have done some reading on it and the best information I can- get is this, that in the United States and in Canada too, agriculture has become big business. The 100 acre farm in the western states and, I think, in western Canada too, is pretty nearly a thing of the past. By the use of improved machinery men are now farming one, two or three thousand acres, and they bring into operation machinery by which one man will do as much work as eight, ten or perhaps a dozen men used to do some years ago.

speechtext:
Agriculture is very different from what it was a few years.ago. The farmers have now a machine that reaps and threshes the grain so that all operations in between reaping and threshing are avoided. Under those conditions farms of thousands of acres can be and are being cultivated, and the reduction in the number of people employed in agriculture in the United States is directly attributable to the enlargement of farms and the improvement of machinery.
If we went back to the old days when we had a reaper with men following it to bind the sheaves and shock them up, in order to produce enough food for this country we would require on the land five times as many people as we have to-day. Agriculture is keeping pace with all other industries and

The Budget-Mr. Hocken
on the farms things are being accomplished to-day that were not dreamed of a few years ago. These things account for the lessening of the population on the farm. While the agricultural population of the United States may have decreased somewhat, the general population of that republic has increased and that country has gone through the most astonishing period of prosperity that it has ever experienced. There is a higher standard of living for all classes, of people; the country is prosperous in the highest degree, and I venture to say the farmers there are sharing in that prosperity. If there is any indebtedness it is probably attributable to the purchase of these costly machines, costing $4,000 or $5,000 a piece, but enabling the farmer to produce that much more and to reduce the unit cost of his product.
My agricultural friends deliver in this House and fill the newspapers with arguments in favour of free trade. But they do not examine the whole question; they do not take into account many factors that ought to be taken into account in arriving at the best policy for this country. As Canadians we ought to ask ourselves this question:	Am I
desirous that this country shall be a great country, have a Burge population and be prosperous? Starting from that point I contend that no country can be truly great on one industry. If my hon. friends had their way and absolute free trade were adopted as the trade policy of Canada, we would get down to one industry.

speechtext: Not at all.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
There is not in any city
in Canada an industry to which my hon. friends would desire to give any protection. If they had their way and absolute free trade were put into effect, this would be solely and only an agricultural country. The greatness of a country depends not on one industry but on a diversity of industries. It depends on many different lines of industry being established and carried on profitably. There is no country of any consequence in the world that attempts to live on agriculture. Admitting that agriculture is the basic and most important industry in the Dominion of Canada, yet I think if those who are engaged in agriculture would look at the question all round, they would discover that if they were going to do their whole duty as Canadians they must give some consideration and some reasonable protection in order to allow other industries to live. There is not in Canada to-day a farmer who has children reaching up to the age of maturity and self-support who does not profit in his family by the existence of a variety
of industries. I wonder how many of my hon. friends opposite who have children who have gone out to make their own way, have children who are engaged in industry or commerce that is due to the existence of those industries in our cities. Let me take the case of a farmer in Ontario, because I know more about that, although I do not know much about farming.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear. *

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I think I know a little
more about farming in Ontario than some of my hon. friends opposite know about the industries in our cities, and I have more regard for the farmer than my hon. friends who would argue in favour of Simon-pure free trade have for those engaged in those industries.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Do farmers in Canada ask the industries of which the hon. member is speaking to tax themselves for the benefit of agriculture?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Whether they ask or not,
they do undoubtedly. The taxes that go to support this government are drawn from industry-

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
-and the concessions
that the farmers get for the small amount they pay per capita in the way of tariff duty more than compensate them for what they have to pay. I say, Sir, that it is in the interest of every farmer in the country that we should have prosperous cities. These cities create openings for those members of the families of farmers who are not adapted to agricultural pursuits and have no taste for agriculture, and if you take a farmer with a family, of five or six children, we will say, more than half of them leave the farm; they are not adapted to farming.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
They all leave the
farms do they not?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Not while they are as
prosperous as they are to-day. So that if we are going to have an all-round country here, we must have cities as well as rural districts.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman arguing that without protection there would be no cities at all, no industries?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I think I can say that
there would be very few cities and those would be of very little account. If my hon. friend had her way and brought free trade into effect-and I think she believes in free trade-the cities of this country would shrivel up.
The Budget-Mr. Hocken

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes, they would shrivel
up. If we were buying our implements and buying our manufactured goods from the other side, as my hon. friends would have us do, what would there be to keep the cities alive? I say that it is much better for the farmer that there should be some communities of considerable size within his reach.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: They constitute local markets.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Not only that, but they
make a vast difference to his social position. The prairies to-day are better districts to live in than they were forty, or thirty, or twenty years ago, because there are cities.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Has not England's
fiscal policy made her great?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
No, protection-protection up to 1846. That is what made her great.
' Mr. HOCKEN:	My hon. friend from
Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) has not read far enough back; he has only read back to the time of Mr. Cobden and Mr. Bright. Let him go farther back and he will find that Great Britain was made preeminently an industrial nation by protection.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
And she is coming
back to it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes, with the Safeguarding of Industries Act and similar legislation. It was only when England gained that position of industrial preeminence and had control of the commerce of the sea, that she found it to her advantage to adopt free trade in order to sell her products abroad and bring raw materials in free. In my judgment England will never recover the preeminence she enjoyed in industry under a free trade policy because every nation in the world is straining in all possible ways to build up its industries and is putting into effect protective policies in order to do that.
Where in history can my hon. friend point to a growth equivalent to that of the United States which has been built up and maintained by protection? And the farmers of that country are stronger protectionists than any other class of people.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: No, no.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I predict that the day
will come, Mr. Speaker, when my hon. friends who sit to my left, or their successors, will be just as keen for protection as the farmers of the United States. I venture to say further that if the agriculturists of Canada, and it is

certainly true of the agriculturists of Ontario, study the whole question of building up a great nation in Canada, they will come to the conclusion that a reasonable measure of protection is as necessary for them as it is for the cities and the towns.
I have only one song to sing as a rule-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
-speaking on the budget, and what I have said is-purely incidental to what I want to say. I wish to say a word for one industry in this country that is perishing because of the disfavour in which it finds itself with the government of the day. I want to bring to the attention of the House the condition of the publishing industry in Canada, and when I say that it is perishing I speak absolutely by the book, for within the last five or ten years the number of publications that have suspended because of inability tq meet competition-foreign competition-runs into the hundreds. I submit that the publishing industry is a great industry, and it is not failing in Canada because of any fault of the men that are engaged in it. I can name to you men who have invested large sums, and who have done their best in trying to produce Canadian magazines teaching Canadian sentiment, trying to further that Canadian spirit of which we have all talked so much and for which we do not seem to feel inclined to do very much. Sir, the blame, in my judgment, lies directly upon the administration, an administration that will not enforce the laws now upon the statute books, will not apply the items which are in the tariff. If the items already in the tariff schedule were applied there would be some hope for Canadian periodical literature, and it is with the "hope that springs eternal in the human breast'' that I want to present the case for the publishing industry again to-day.
I would like hon. members first to consider the character of that industry. It is not like the manufacture of a machine, or of wearing apparel, or of anything that is in general use. This industry is one upon which Canadian sentiment must be built; it goes deeper than the manufacture of any goods that are in general use. It goes right into the minds and hearts of the people, and if we are going to develop a country with a sentiment of our own, and to inculcate a real Canadian spirit in our young people, then we must -have some kind of a vehicle for the purpose, and the best vehicle that I can think of is a periodica] press.

The Budget-Mr. Hocken

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Would not the daily newspaper meet that need to a very large extent?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I think not. The daily
newspaper gives us the news, and contains an occasional political article or a neutral article, but it is essentially a presentation of the news of the day, of the happenings of the world. It does, of course, express Canadian sentiment, but not at all in the way that a periodical press does. The man who writes for the daily paper writes of the hour; his articles must be composed in an hour, or in a few hours at most. The man who writes for the periodical press takes weeks or months, takes whatever time is necessary to prepare his article to his own satisfaction, and he produces a form of literature that is much more effective in developing a national sentiment than anything a newspaper man can write. My hon. friend in the chair will see the force of the statement I make. I say, Sir, that that is the only agency we have for contributing to the education of the masses and building up a strong national sentiment among Canadians, and for stimulating that sentiment. Surely it must be admitted that this is desirable from every standpoint. If we are going to remain Canada, we must be Canadians. We must have some special idea in our heads as to our own nationality. We cannot imbibe the ideals of a foreign state without suffering in our own sentiment, and that is the situation in which we find ourselves to-day. All that is best in this periodical literature that floods our country is pro-United States. There are 70,000,000 copies of American periodicals coming into this country every year, not one of them telling the Canadian story, all of them leaving the impression that God's country is the United States, and putting into the minds of our young people the idea that the land of promise is over the border, not here. It is one of those agencies that have done so much to attract the best we have.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Unfortunately,
one of the difficulties is that the Conservative party have been trying to make everybody believe that.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Order.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I did not quite get what
the hon. gentleman said. I am free to admit that there are a great many admirable magazines coming in here from the. United States, but at the best they teach United States: they do not teach Canada. They stimulate the idea in our young people, and in some of our middle-aged people, to seek for
those green fields far away, and it is one of the means that has been effective in attracting so many of our young Canadians over the border. From every province in Canada they slip across, and while it is very flattering to us to know that almost any Canadian can get a situation in the United States, it is not very encouraging to those of us who want to see a great country built up here, populous, prosperous and powerful, as it can be, and as I hope it will be. But the day is being delayed, and the attractions of the United States are being presented to our people by this flood of literature that comes in.
And at the worst, Mr. Speaker, we have admitted to this country to-day the most pernicious literature that is published on this continent, perhaps on any continent. Certainly nothing could be much worse than what is published in the United States and sent in here free. I am going to read to you what the Washington correspondent of the Baltimore Sun said about this class of publication in the United States. Writing to the Independent, of Boston, he said:
And not only have we produced a great smut crop of a coarseness peculiarly our own, but the more obscene of the French papers have now been translated into English and appear on the news stands along with the originals. When you stop to analyze, scrutinize, and check up, there is here presented more reason for apprehension as to the future than any other single symptom in America to-day.
The place to fully appreciate its proportions is in the smaller cities and towns, with populations ranging from 20,000 up to 100,000-towns, for instance, like Fairmont, West Virginia, where one news dealer sells 2,200 copies of every issue of a single monthly, exclusively devoted to stories of sex experiences and the nude in art; or like Steubenville, Ohio, where out of 110 periodicals on sale in a single store, 60 were either out-and-out a prurient type or bordered on the libidinous line.
Tt is not the cheap and sexually suggestive fiction magazines, although these are many and rotten, that constitute the real shock troops of these paper battalions of literary indecency, so much as the smaller and more compact nonfiction affairs frankly and exclusively given over to obscenities. Some of these are published in Chicago, some in Philadelphia, but most of them in Newark, New Jersey, and are issued by the same individuals under different corporate names. They mainly contain a rehash of the dirty stories and jokes told in the smoking rooms of pullman cars or hotel lobbies.
Some of my hon. friends may say: You are talking about the United States. Well, Mr. Speaker, I went down to Sparks street during the lunch hour, and I went into only one store, but I picked up a few samples of the kind of stuff that is coming into this country from the United States. Here is one
The Budget-Mr. Hocken

of them-Sea Breezes. Shocking, isn't it? Any member of this House can go down to Sparks street and buy this magazine. I do not suppose any member would buy it, unless he had a purpose, but the truth is that the youth of the city are buying it. Young people are going through the pages of a thing like that.
Then I picked up another one, and the title itself, I think, condemns this one-Sex Stories. That is admitted free, contrary to the very item of the tariff. I wish my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Euler) were here. There is a book unfit to be sold in any store in the city of Ottawa or anywhere else for that matter, but it is Canada we are concerned1 with.
Here is another-True Experiences-another of the sex story magazines. This kind of stuff, bound, as you see, in different sections, comes into this country free, in violation of three different items of the tariff.
So, at its worst, Mr. Speaker, it is about as bad as it could be. I could get you sixty other magazines of the same type, only I did not want to spend that much money, and I thought these three samples ought to be sufficient to convince the House that a kind of literature is coming in here with the approval of our customs officials and of the government that ought to be excluded.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Would the hon member advocate barring that class of magazine from the country?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I certainly would.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Thank you.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: In the United States, Mr. Speaker, they do everything they can think of to stop this flood of literature. They suppress a magazine, and the next week it appears under a different name.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am heartily in sympathy
with some of the views expressed by the hon. member, but would it not be well to take this up as a single problem, rather than complicate it with questions of the customs tariff?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I would think, Mr. Speaker, that the present laws against Obscene literature would exclude this kind of stuff. It is within the power of the Customs department to exclude these magazines now, on the ground of Obscenity, but they come in free, and are part of that great flood of literature to which I object coming in in the way it does, to the destruction of our own peri-

odical literature, and to the destruction of a very important industry in this country. The voice of Canada, as it can be expressed in a periodical press, is stifled because our magazines are absolutely unable to compete with those in the United States serving a community of 120,000,000 of people.
The conditions which are maintained at the present time render it quite impossible to establish a distinctly Canadian periodical press. We have in our customs tariff three items; one that provides that on all advertising matter coming into this country from the United States a duty of fifteen cents a pound shall be charged. That is not enforced. I have before me a magazine of 204 pages, mostly advertising, all of which ought to pay fifteen cents a pound under our own tariff, but this comes in free, not only competing with our own magazines, but by the advertising competing with every paper in Canada through the great volume of advertising they put in. I submit further with regard to this magazine and others of the same class that the dumping duty should be applied. This magazine weighs a pound and a half. I weighed it myself. The raw paper in the rolls is worth nine cents, and it is sold in the stores of this city for five cents. The dealer buys it for three cents. Here we have nine cents worth of white paper beautifully printed and bound, the type set up, and articles paid for, and it comes into Canada at three cents to the dealer and five cents to the purchaser.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
What does it
sell for in the United States?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Five cents.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Then how can
you apply the dumping duty?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Nine cents' worth of paper is sold for three cents, and if that does not come within the dumping clause, then the act should be amended so that it will come within it. No Canadian can advertise in this magazine. It has a circulation of about 80,000 in Canada, but it has a total circulation of over a million, and the Canadian advertiser who would pay for a million circulation would get only 100,000, or less. Canadian advertisers, therefore, are excluded from this publication; they are excluded from the Saturday Evening Post and the Ladies Home Journal, because they cannot get more than 100.000 circulation, or 130.000. I think, in the case of the Saturday Evening Post. But if they advertise they have to pay for a circulation of a million. In the first place we have a duty of fifteen cents a pound that should be applied to magazines

The Budget

Mr. Hocken
of this class, because while a certain amount of reading matter which is admitted free is mixed up with advertising, these periodicals are essentially advertising publications. They are not published primarily as literature, but as advertising mediums and should be treated as such by the Customs department of this country. Now another item in our tariff says:
Books, viz, novels, works of fiction or literature of a similar character, unbound or paper bound, or in sheets:
British preferential tariff, 15 per cent; Intermediate, 22J per cent; General tariff, 25 per cent.
I submit that all the magazines that come here should pay the twenty-five per cent rate under that item. There is the item in the tariff; they do not enforce it, but they fall back upon another item, No. 184, which reads:
Newspapers, and quarterly, monthly and semimonthly magazines, and weekly literary papers, unbound, free.
You will notice it says "unbound". Here is a magazine, a very decent one too, and the Customs department says that is unbound. It has sixteen sections. These sections have to be collated and stitched, the cover put on, and more work is done in the bindery than is done in the pressroom on this magazine, and yet our Customs department says it is unbound. I do not know how that can be defended. But if this publication were treated as it should be instead of being admitted free under item No. 184, it would pay twenty-five per cent, and if it paid twenty-five per cent, it would be something of a discouragement to the American magazines in their effort to capture the whole of the Canadian market. I do not say this magazine ought to be kept out but if we have an item in the tariff providing that it shall pay twenty-five per cent, it should pay that amount, while the British magazines would come in under the preferential tariff of fifteen per cent. I am not asking for any special or further protection for magazines. I say apply the tariff as it stands. I suggested last year that, instead of charging fifteen cents a pound on advertising matter, a general rate of ten cents a pound on the whole magazine should be applied. I did that because the customs officials state that it is impossible to separate the advertising in a magazine like this from the reading matter. Of course that is not impossible at all. It is done in the United States for postal purposes, but it means a certain amount of work for every one that comes in; so last year, instead of sticking to the demand for fifteen cents a pound, I suggested ten cents a pound as being
easier to collect. I want fifteen cents on the advertising, or I want twenty-five per cent, according to item 169 in the tariff.
If we have a tariff that can be interpreted exactly the opposite of what it says, what is the sense of it? It does not accomplish anything at all.
While these publications are admitted free into Canada, the Canadian publisher has to pay duty on everything that he uses. He has to pay on his paper, he has to pay on his machinery and he has to pay on his electrotypes. I have ninety-one items here in the tariff that enter into the publisher's business which are dutiable, and he comes then into competition with people who pay no duty. He is forced up against the free list of American magazines. I have the record here of one periodical published in the city of Toronto. This publisher could go to Buffalo, buy his paper, print it, get all his electrotypes and everything, and he could save $490 on every issue, as compared with the cost of publishing in the city of Toronto. He could save 85,583 dollars a year if, instead of doing his printing in Toronto, he took it over to Buffalo. In the first place, he has to pay a duty of twenty-five per cent on his paper. Paper is cheaper there than in Canada. He can buy paper in Buffalo and lay it down in Toronto, and when he gets it in Toronto it is exactly the same price as the co3t of the paper in Buffalo, with the duty and the freight added, and that is about a cent and a half a pound. That is a very heavy impost upon the publisher of that magazine-$490 an issue, besides all his equipment. I have a list of ninety-one different articles entering into the business of the publisher. The tariff runs all the way from 10 per cent to 35 per cent, everything the man uses is taxed, and then he comes into unhampered competition with the American publisher.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Is my hon. friend complaining of that tariff?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
No. I say the papermakers and other manufacturers ought to enjoy enough protection to keep them alive; but I say further the publisher ought to get some protection too; he at least ought to get the protection that is now contained in our own tariff.
How the Minister of Finance can justify the present interpretation of the items in the customs tariff is absolutely beyond my comprehension. I am confident that if the government took a fair and reasonable view they would at least say: We will adopt item 169 of the customs tariff and charge 25 per cent
The Budget-Mr. Hocken

on all these magazines. That would not exclude a single American magazine; but it would do this. The Saturday Evening Post has started a subscription campaign in order to get a circulation in Canada of 200,000 copies. A tariff of 25 per cent would simply discourage that campaign and would leave the publishers of that paper to take the natural circulation that they may get. At the present time they are spending enormous sums of money in forcing the circulation of the Saturday Evening Post-all to the detriment of existing Canadian publications, and it is a most unfair position in which to put our publishers. .
I can conceive, Mr. Speaker, that if the publishing industry were given a fair deal we would have more ink-makers, perhaps we would have another paper mill or .two, and the general industry surrounding and cognate to the publishing industry would benefit correspondingly. Of course, the automobile manufacturers gelt their raw materials free, so do the implement manufacturers, -but the publishers get nothing. The publishers are not asking particularly for free raw materials, they are willing that those with whom they deal should have reasonable protection

what Mr. Marler used to call "a cost of living" tariff; but they claim that this country should be protected against the flood of 300 different magazines that come in here every time they are issued.
It may be interesting to the House to know that 25,000,000 pounds of advertising printing comes into Canada from the United States free of duty every year. If we applied our tariff on that 25,000,000 pounds we would get in duty $375,000 at the 15-cen-t rate which I have mentioned. That indicates the handicap under which our publishers are working. It is equivalent to this government paying a bounty to the American publisher to compete with the Canadian publisher. That is exactly the position. If conditions were reversed, if Canadian periodical literature was going into the United States in anything like a comparable volume, the United States government would put on a tariff over night. They would not stand for that, they would not permit their people to be fed up with Canadian literature as we permit our people to be fed up with American literature. It must be borne in mind that if we put on a duty of 25 per cent the price of the Saturday Evening Post would not be increased at all; its publishers would absorb that tax. Horn, members may be surprised to hear that the total _ weight of the Saturday Evening Post sent into Canada in 1926 amounted to 8,978,944 pounds.

A tremendous volume of this paper is also sent in here through the mails and is carried by the Canadian post office for nothing; we get nothing at all out of the postage. Altogether 659,275 copies of American mag-azines are carried by the -Canadian mails for which our government gets nothing at all-not a cent. The total circulation per issue of these magazines is 1,468,886 copies. Some of them are weeklies, some monthlies, but per issue we have a million and a -half copies of American -publications coming into this country free, in defiance of our own customs tariff. In other words, we buy eight American magazines for every Canadian magazine bought in this -country.
Every .person who knows anything about the publishing business and certain newspapers have taken notice of this state of things, and they all agree it is about time that something was done by the government to at least give sufficient protection to our Canadian publishers to enable them to live and build up a Canadian literature. The Kitchener Record, the paper of -the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Euler)-I am sorry he is not in his seat-says:
Acting upon the contention that the Canadian publishing trade is suffering from outside competition, the delegation suggests the imposing of a tariff of 10 cents a pound on all periodicals and week end magazines entering Canada. It is estimated that the consequent revenue would be approximately $5,000,000.
I should like to read to the House what the Globe says on this subject:
Sooner or later the Canadian government will be obliged to take cognizance of the vast circulation of United States publications in this country. They are strangling the publishing industry here, depriving Canadian -workers of millions of dollars' worth of employment; they are "Americanizing" Canada by means of the reading material offered; they must have a very grave effect on Canadian industry in general, owing to the tremendous amount of advertising of United States products carried in their columns.
The Globe puts into a paragraph practically my whole argument, and I think it should be considered very carefully and sympathetically by the government. The Orillia Packet, which is a very well edited weekly paper, says:
By all means let us have a duty on the American publications that are flooding Canada to the extent of more than a million copies a week. It is one new tax to which no objection can be taken.
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, that I can have any influence with my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, but I have pleaded with him, I have beseeched him, and I have said everything I can think of to convince him

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
of the justice of what the publishers are asking for. All I am requesting him to do now is to see that his colleague the Minister of Customs applies the tariff we now have against these magazines. I ask him to suggest to his colleague that item 169 should not be interpreted as classing as unbound a magazine of the kind I am now holding up for him to look at. I do not know whether the minister saw this magazine. It contains sixteen different sections, all collated, all bound. There is more work in the bindery than in the printing. Yet that is classed by the Customs department as unbound-manifestly an indefensible interpretation. If the hon. minister would take enough time to go into this question with reasonable care I think he would discover that what the magazine publishers are asking for is not only reasonable, but something that cannot be evaded and the evasion defended.
I submit, Sir, as I have done on former occasions, that this is one industry that should receive consideration at the hands of the government. It is not asking much, only what is on the book; and if my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) will grant this request, he will do something at least to support a movement which will make for a better and a more prosperous periodical press in Canada than we have at the present time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
For
once I find myself in complete accord with my hon. friend from Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hoeken) in the desire to protect the youth of the country from the filthy literature-is it literature?-which at .present comes from the United States and is sold throughout Canada in the cities and towns, in the stores, at the street corners, everywhere. I think, however, that the hon. gentleman might have addressed his remarks to the House generally rather than to one particular quarter. Last year partly at my request, the late Minister of Customs excluded the filthiest and most obnoxious of these American magazines, and the first thing that was done by the shortlived government, which was put into power, in the name of virtue, in the month of June, was to admit again those very undesirable publications. I do not bring this as an argument against any party. I simply join hands with the hon. member in requesting the Minister of Customs to take steps to keep out literature of this sort. If the minister does not do so of his own good will he will hear more about the matter. He should apply again the regulation or, as I believe, the order in council, or the order of the Customs department, which was put into force by the late Mr. Boivin.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Can my hon. friend give
us some information regarding that order in council of which he speaks? On whose recommendation was the publication in question banned? I never heard of the matter before, and I should like to look into it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am not sure that it
is an order in council; but I know that last year the late Mr. Boivin, then Minister of Customs, issued orders to prohibit the entry into Canada of such filthy rags as the Daily Mirror and publications of that nature. And these publications were stopped. The moment the succeeding government came into power, however, the publications in question were allowed in again. That is all I know about the matter.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Are they still coming in?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes, you will find them at every street corner in Montreal and Ottawa; and the school children are buying them every afternoon. They are the filthiest and most degrading kind of reading. As every hon. member knows, I do not believe in promoting virtue by means of laws; but I may point out that in England, where more than anywhere else in the world, personal liberty in these .matters has been preserved, parliament has passed legislation prohibiting the dissemination of such reading matter. Lately, one of the Labour representatives in the British parliament was in the United States, and he made the sensible observation that before the American people attempted to make men sober by law, they should see to it that the minds of the youth of the country were not degraded to the degree they are to-day in the United States. In that respect I am absolutely in accord with the sentiments of my hon. friend, and I am prepared to support any movement that tends to protect the youth of Canada against the influence of such publications.
With regard to the other aspect of the question, with which the hon. member ha3 dealt in a very interesting manner, that of protecting the publishing industry, it should be brought to the attention of the tariff board. I do not think this is the proper time to discuss that question from the various points of view that can be advanced. Again I entirely agree with the hon. member that everything should be done to foster a national sentiment, but I fear that in many ways we are not adopting the right means. You will not build up a national sentiment by means of a protected literature. If you take other means to that end, if you direct the minds of the youth, to whatever race or province
The Budget

Mr. Bourassa

they belong, to the fact that Canada is their country, and not France, not England, not the British Empire, then in a generation or two you may have something like unanimity among Canadians in regard to their common nationality. Thereafter a literature with a national sentiment will develop. I do not know that a national sentiment has ever been created anywhere by literature, nor that literature has ever been fostered by means of tariff protection. If in the school, in the family and in all our social and political activities, we appeal to the one sentiment of devotion to Canada as our common country, we shall create the mental and moral material upon which a national literature will grow. I do not know how it goes in the English-speaking provinces;1 but according to the hon. gentleman himself, as he spoke here last year, similarity of language with the United States makes the people more open to the penetration of American ideals and thought. I can say however that, so far as our own province is concerned, more or fewer papers coming from another country would not affect in the slightest degree our conception of Canadianism. This may suggest that something else is wrong with the English provinces in the matter of fostering a national sentiment. I will not however dwell on that point now. The hon. member is to be congratulated upon having raised the subject, and I trust that this is not the last occasion on which he will have brought it up.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Not unless we get relief.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
There is another point
of view from which the question may be discussed. American publications, and Canadian as well, which take advantage of the low rates offered by the Post Office Department to disseminate throughout Canada what are practically advertising catalogues, are a detriment to the ordinary trade of the towns and villages. The spread of -this advertising matter throughout the country has had something to do with the crisis through which local trade in the small towns and villages has been passing for many years.
With regard to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), It find myself in this position, that while agreeing almost entirely with the opinions expressed by the hon. member as well as by the member for Southeast Grey (.Miss Mac-phail), I cannot bring myself to the point of supporting the amendment, for the simple reason that the first paragraph censures the government for not dealing with the tariff at this session, notwithstanding that it was unanimously agreed last session that the whole

question of the tariff should be submitted to a commission of inquiry. On this question, therefore, I take exactly the same ground I took a few days ago on another subject. The House, in the exercise of its supreme jurisdiction, has seen fit to create a body to gather data and secure information to enable us to deal with the tariff in a satisfactory manner and with some measure of expert knowledge at our disposal. I hope that the tariff board will not rest content with receiving petitions from certain industries for more protection and, therefore, with looking at the question from a purely industrial point of view. Last year I ventured to suggest that it was not only the tariff question that should be studied thoroughly from an expert and economic point of view, but the whole problem of taxation as connected, not only with paying our debt and meeting our fixed charges, not only with the balancing of our Budget as between revenues and expenditures, but mainly with regard to the situation of the various communities, the different classes of people in Canada who contribute to the prosperity of the country, and to find out whether they suffer or not from the systems of taxation that we have adooted from time to time without much thought, I am afraid, being given to the interlocking of the various parts of the fiscal machinery.
When that is done, of course the government will have to take their stand. I have much personal friendship and sympathy for our Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). He is a canny Scotchman, and next to my race and my province, the Scotch people an<d Scotland are very close to my heart. But a canny Scotchman must not push diplomacy too far. The time is soon coming when the hon. gentleman and his colleagues will have to choose whether they belong to highland or to lowland. In his native country there were a few highlanders and a few lowlanders who, after having stolen each other's cattle, found a new country, no man's land, which separated the lowlands of Scotland from England, There they changed somewhat their patriotic occupation, and they alternately plundered the highlands and lowlands, and the land of the southron or the Sassenach. '
After the inquiry has been completed, the government will have to make its choice as between-I do not say no tariff: nobody, I think, advocates that at the present time- but as between tending towards low tariff and freer trade, or stability of tariff as upheld by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) for example, and a stiff increase in the tariff as recommended by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett).

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
I could leave the matter there, and logically I should not discuss the tariff, since I consider the House is not in a position to pass judgment upon it. But in view of certain declarations that have been made in this House by members of all parties this session, last session, and during the two election campaigns through which we have passed, I wish to place myself on record emphatically-and I will do it upon every occasion-against the idea that the province of Quebec stands for a high tariff. It has never done so in the past. It is less so favourable to-day, and the time is, I think, soon coming when not only the rural population of Quebec, but a fast growing number of thinking people in the cities will realize that the protective system, as applied so far, has done just as much harm to rural Quebec and eventually to the whole of that province as it may have done to the west or the maritime provinces.
When the government make their choice, if they are in need of scientific argumentation against the principle of protection, against the application of protection, they will find ample argument in that extraordinary address which was delivered to us a few days ago by the hon. member for West Calgary. With the little knowledge I have of economics, I admit I remain dumbfounded. I greatly admire the talents, the brilliancy and the versatility of the hon. member. In fact, he found it possible within the scope of one oration to bid fairly and boldly for leadership either of unalloyed Tory imperialism or of Simon-pure Liberalism, and he ended practically with an offer to socialism. The hon. gentleman is quite fit, I admit, to lead any and every party. Was it a warning to the future convention to be held in Winnipeg, that if the perpetually renascent Conservative party do not take advantage of the shining lights they have at their disposal, some of those shining lights may find their way elsewhere? I do not know.
But not only did the hon. gentleman base his very interesting and convincing argument with regard to the principles of taxation upon that prophet and precursor of the Manchester school which gave free trade to England1- Adam Smith - but he out-Heroded Adam Smith. He added two principles to the famous four principles once enunciated by the father of free trade. Those two are that taxation, to be properly laid down, to be beneficial both to the country and to the individual, must be universal and visible. This stands as the most direct condemnation of the principle of protection that can be imagined. If there is one form of taxation which is not and which cannot be universal, it is a customs 32649-39
tariff, at least as we have applied it. If there is one form of taxation which the ratepayer cannot measure, cannot count, so that to him it is not visible, it is that form of taxation which he never pays himself, but which he reimburses to the government or to the protected manufacturer through the retail dealer to whom he goes to get all his necessities of life.
I think I could discern, in listening to and reading that very excellent address, that perhaps the hon. gentleman thought that we could combine, as it has at all times been, held, although somewhat paradoxically, I think, the principle of free trade and the principle of protection, just as the United States have done. I know it has been an argument frequently used in the past and sometimes used in the present by upholders of a protective tariff. Strange to say, that argument and that example have been mostly, if not exclusively, used1 by members of that party which, for the last twenty-five years at least, have been posing before the people of this country and the people of the empire as the staunchest upholders of all British institutions. Its stand always is: We should do as the United States have done; if we imitate the United States we will reach the same result.
I do not want to dwell at length upon that. But if we reflect a few minutes upon the differences in conditions-climatic, geographical, economic, ethnical-we will realize that even if we should copy to the letter, in every item of our tariff, or in any other part of our fiscal legislation, the policy of the United States, we could not reach the same results. Because we are not similarly situated; because there are many raw materials required by our protected or non-protected industries that we must perforce and for all times import. Therefore the idea that Canada can be a self-contained and a self-sufficient country is nullified at the beginning by the very conditions of the country itself- conditions which no government, no party, no policy, can change or will ever change.
With regard to the effect of the tariff on the peopling of this country, I have heard that question discussed for the last thirty-five years at least. I remember my old friend Sir Wilfrid Laurier telling me that in making his maiden speech in the legislature at Quebec, in 1872 I think it was, he had denounced the Conservative government because of the migration of our population to the United States. I remember well the time between 1891 and 1896, when this country was passing through very dire commercial, agricultural and industrial crises, when we Liberals were denouncing the Conservative

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa

party because protection had ruined this country, because protection had uprooted the rural population of our provinces and brought them to the large industrial centres; and because, when the crisis came, if they did not go back to the country they took the road to the United States. There are many causes for the migration of our population from Canada to the United States. There are those permanent causes to which I have just alluded with regard to our fiscal policy, permanent causes which it is absurd to ignore. The Climate of Canada as compared to that of the United States is of itself an impediment. The geographical division of the country is in itself an impediment. I once defined Canada, as it has been carved by diplomats, by politicians, on both sides of the ocean, without any regard to the future, without any regard to the national exigencies of the countary, as "a geographical absurdity." But that is done. Does it mean that we cannot face the issue and remedy it? No; but it means we have some obstacles to vanquish; it means that we should exercise more patience, it means that we cannot hope to see this country grow to the same degree of amplitude as the United States have grown during the century that has passed. It means also-and for many, many years to come., probably for all time to come-that vast portions of our country, especially the western portions, will always have to export an immense quantity of farm products for which they have the right to demand the easiest market, the largest and most varied number of markets, in the easiest and cheapest manner; and we, as Canadians, have the duty to help them in getting them as much as we can.
With regard to the maritimes, well, one of of the late colleagues of some of the hon. gentlemen sitting on the other side, a true old Tory, Mr. McCurdy, in several articles and lectures, endeavoured to prove, and I think did prove somewhat successfully, that the application of the protective policy had practically ruined all the small industries of his province; that Nova Scotia had suffered from protection and by protection, because the application of protection to the conditions of our country had concentrated the large industries mainly in the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec-I would go further and say mainly in some of the large centres of Quebec, and more so in various centres of Ontario-and had ruined all the small local industries of the maritime provinces. I am not a judge as to that, but here surely is testimony that cannot be allowed to go by the board without being examined. So that 
taking into account the conditions of all parts of the country, taking into account those permanent conditions to which I have referred- the configuration of the country, as well as the lack of population which we cannot hope to remedy in a few years-Canada must for a great number of years look to foreign markets to export the vast surplus of her farm products. And if we want to get foreign markets, and many of them, we must be prepared to deal fairly with those countries where we will find such markets. The hon. member for West Calgary made an argument which I think is sound. He said we should look rather to those countries where our products are needed than to those that will take Them simply on account of some treaty we may make with them. As a general proposition that is quite true, but it has to be scrutinized. All our surplus products, either agricultural or industrial, will not be needed all the time in one country or in a few countries. Conditions change elsewhere as they do here. The conditions of production differ; the wage-earning power of various countries changes; the value of the money of a foreign country changes, and has changed tremendously since the war. But the hon. member for West Calgary said that if we relied upon foreign markets for the exportation of our products, we may find ourselves-by a stroke of the pen or in a single night-deprived of those markets and thereby our trade and industrial conditions will be entirely upset. I think this is an argument in favour of looking for as many markets as we can get, because we cannot suppose that if we export our wheat to ten countries instead of four we shall be in more danger than if we look only to one market. You cannot suppose that a country will agree to trade with us, either by treaty or by necessity, and then change its policy just as a matter of caprice as the hon. member said. You cannot reasonably anticipate that if you deal with twenty countries instead of ten, those twenty countries will gather together and arrive at a decision to close their markets to our product just for the sake of making good the argument of the hon. gentleman.
But where I could not follow the hon. gentleman was the application he made of that argument to the policy pursued by the government in trying to make treaties. The argument applies to a certain degree to countries that take our produce of necessity- precisely the contrary of what he said-and which by a change in their tariff, if they see fit, may change our conditions. But I have always understood that, all the world over, the purpose of trade treaties was precisely to

The. Budget-Mr. Bourassa
create and maintain for a certain number of years certain conditions of stability between the two parties to the treaty. When we made the reciprocity treaty with the United States in 1854, it was made for ten years with the proviso that it could not be terminated except on two years' notice; so that for at least twelve years we knew with what conditions we had to deal, so far as the United States was concerned; and the very proof of the unsoundness of the argument of the hon. gentleman is, that enumerating a number of countries with which we have trade treaties at the present time, he mentioned the fact that the United States at a certain time adopted a stiff tariff against our products. Precisely; we had no treaty with the United States.
But there is one point which has been touched upon by the hon. gentleman, and I think neglected by most other speakers, upon which I want to put myself on record once more, and that is with reference to our preferential trade. The hon. gentleman grew enthusiastic on that point. He let us see the dawn of the day when the whole British Empire would be a self-sustaining and self-contained empire. He reminded us of the patient gathering of figures by Lord Long. Lord Long was a very able man; but as a practical politician able to get a policy through, there was one man connected with that idea who was far stronger than Lord Long, and that was Mr. Joseph Chamberlain. It does not mean, because the famous trade reform campaign turned so stiffly against the Tory and Unionist party in England that tariff reform will never come about; but I think some facts that came out then prove to us that if there is an unrealizable policy, or one absolutely uncertain, it is that idea of an inter-imperial trade union. Always as in the United States, the hon. gentleman said. Again I repeat, if Canada cannot expect in the application of a protective policy to reap the same results which the United States have reaped, because of the differences in conditions between the two countries, to a far greater extent is it futile and idle to think that the British possessions scattered over the five continents, separated by the seven seas, composed of all climates and races, can ever come to a common policy in any matter whatever that can be conceived. You may say that precisely because of the diversity of conditions which exist between the various countries of the British Empire, the British Empire can be self-sustaining. Theoretically, yes, if you can bring all those countries together and make them stick together as do 32649-394
the fifty states of the American union. Quite so, but precisely because each of the countries of the British Empire has closer neighbours than other British countries, has trade relations, and intellectual relations, good or bad, such as those that have been described this afternoon by the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken), it is idle and futile to think that you will ever get them to agree upon one empire policy. Therefore, we have to fall back upon the somewhat lame and, I may say, absurd policy which we have been practising for the last thirty years.
One very curious thing about that policy, Mr. Speaker, is to find that the three parties at present dividing public opinion in Canada are agreed upon it. The high protectionists are in favour of maintaining the British preference; the freer trade party, as the Liberal party is supposed to be, are also in favour of maintaining that preference; but to my astonishment, gentlemen on the other side who are bent upon the ideal, which they may reach one of these days, of absolute free trade are also in favour not only of maintaining but increasing the British preference. Have they never thought that the strongest argument in fact which they can leave in the hands of the protectionists of this country is the maintenance and increase of the British preference? Do they know how it was originated? I can tell them.
I was then a young member of this House. In 1896, as in some years previous and some years after, the Liberal party had denounced protection as organized theft and robbery. At the same time, some of the organizers of the Liberal party had received subscriptions from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and had pledged themselves that the program of the party would never be applied. So the poor leaders of the party were divided between their public utterances and the private engagements that had thus been made. Something had to be done. That is always the argument used by party leaders in those circumstances-'something must foe done'- and they adopted that device of the British preference. They said:	We will grant a
preference to British goods, and not only to British goods, but to the goods of all countries that will offer us terms equivalent or as nearly advantageous. There was some sense in that. It was based on a policy of reciprocity. It was a policy inspired by the idea of looking for markets everywhere.
Three years later, under the excitement of the South African war, it was decided to put the stamp of patriotism on that policy. Not Canadian patriotism, no; but the stamp of imperial patriotism. The old policy of

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
Sir John Macdonald, that of a true national policy for the benefit of the people of Canada and the protection of Canadian industries against British as well as foreign competition, was discarded, of course;, by the newly formed and inspired Tory-Imperialistic party; and the Liberals who then and later had a disposition to follow suit weakly, the Liberals -partially Tory, partially protectionist, partially imperialistic, partially everything- thought they would go about half way between the attitude of the Tory party and their own past promises, and thus we went on.
Now wiiat has been the result? The maintenance of the British preference is practically the only cause for the agitation for a higher tariff, so far as our large industries are concerned. Take the woollen industry, or the boot and shoe industry. Talk with those men in private. I know a good many of them. I took up this question twenty-five years ago when I was in this parliament, and I know several of the most important manufacturers of boots and shoes in the province of Quebec. Privately they all tell you that if the British preference were done away with they would not demand a higher tariff, as their present protection would be sufficient But in order to keep in line with the false sentiment that was at the basis of that policy they say:	We have no objection to the
maintenance of the British preference provided you raise the general tariff. The same with the woollen industry.
But if you intend to maintain that British preference, why not apply it honestly and in a practical manner? I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce mentioned the other day that the Australians-and quite properly -in the application of their treaty with us demanded, for example, that automobiles, in order to come under the treaty tariff, should be manufactured in Canada to at least fifty per cent of their value. If I am not mistaken, in the application of the preference, they exact 75 per cent of British value, either in raw material or in labour, before they consider the goods as being imported from Great Britain and entitled to the preferential tariff. Here we do not follow that principle. A personal friend of mine, interested in a very large business, travelling in France, Belgium and Germany a couple of years after the war, saw there in foreign factories woollen goods stamped in advance " British made goods They were made in Germany, they were made in Belgium and they were made in France and shipped to England. A little surplus work was done upon them in England and they were reshipped to Canada as

British-made goods. I think that kind of competition is unfair and dishonest. If we wish to have a British preference, let it be a truly " British " preference; but let us not permit the British trader, at the expense of both the English and Canadian labourer, profiting by the cheaper labour of the continental countries; to impose upon us under false pretences merchandise which is neither British nor Canadian, but foreign made.
But I go further. The time will soon come when, recovering our senses, we will do as all other countries have done, and make our choice either for a protective tariff pure and simple, as Macdonald and Tupper conceived it and applied it-a purely Canadian protective policy-or we will make up our minds that, considering the conditions of our country as they exist and the need of a larger market from year to year for our farm products, we are not going to sacrifice those advantages for the maintenance of a few artificial industries, and at the same time enforce upon our people the necessity of buying at a higher-price goods which they could get elsewhere, especially those goods which are made of raw material not coming from the soil of Canada, and which the soil of Canada will never produce. That is all I have to say upon that question for this year, but I want to place myself on record and protest once more against the assertion that Quebec stands as one with Ontario on that question. I will go further and say that I believe that there is an increasing number of people in Ontario who realize that the protective policy has not given to the country at large what it promised.
As far as the province of Quebec is concerned, I pledge my word in that regard. I have known my province for many years. I have carried on not only political campaigns but various campaigns of education on many subjects. I know rural Quebec perhaps better than urban Quebec, but I know the people of the cities also; and I say the number of people in the province of Quebec who realize that the so-called national policy has not given to us yet what it has promised is growing. I do not say that we are prepared, by a stroke of the pen, as the hon. member for West Calgary has suggested, to upset our policy. No. Sensible people must take account of facts and of created-I will not say created rights-but industries developed, giving employment to a large number of people. I think I can fairly claim for the people of my province that they are pretty sensible on the whole. They may not agree with the member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) upon many aspects of the national

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
spirit, but I think on the whole we have proven that in matter of economics and matters of financial administration we are pretty sensible. We are not so apt to jump at every new idea that is proposed. We are very careful before we accept clap-trap. On the whole the province of Quebec is the best situated of the whole Dominion, financially, economically and socially speaking. From that point of view the province of Quebec is not prepared to jump one way or the other, but it is prepared more than ever, to listen to good reason whether it comes from Saskatchewan, Alberta or Nova Scotia, when we are asked to revise our fiscal policy in order to suit the needs of the whole of Canada. The province of Quebec is more convinced than ever that from a French Canadian point of view, or an all Canadian point of view, agriculture is the important industry of the country. We feel that the spirit of the rural population is certainly the safest for the country to rely upon.
I am not so sure of the argument that we must create by artificial means more industries in our country. We have already too many. What we want is an adjustment of industries. What we want is an adjustment of the capitalization of industries, an adjustment of wealth as between industrial interests, tradesmen, farmers and various classes. In other words, what we want is the introduction of certain principles by which we can arrive at a proper adjustment in matters financial, material and economic. If I could revise the utterances of Adam Smith I would say that, over and above the four principles enunciated by Adam Smith a hundred and fifty years ago, and the two principles enunciated by hi3 successor in this House, I would say that the main thing in view in our whole dealings in the fiscal and financial field is that we should not think of the wealth of any class, but of the maintenance of the family. That was the great fault of the Manchester school. They thought of the individual. They were essentially individualists. They rendered great service in freeing the individual from the yoke of monarchy, from the yoke of autocracy, from the yoke of aristocracy; but, unfortunately, they did that with a view of bringing in the individual considered by himself, either as a ratepayer or as a citizen. But we must come to the right and sound view that the maintenance of the family, of the family spirit, of the family prosperity, is the basis of all sound society. If we do that, if we maintain what we have, especially in the province of Quebec, of the social spirit, created and developed in a well-organized family,
we will have done more to resist the spirit of American absorption, of American imperialism, of American mentality, than by any rate of customs tariff applied.to this quantity of magazines and newspapers.
Now, with regard to the rest of the budget,
I must confess that there I stand, I will not say in glorious isolation, but in noble minority with my friends opposite on almost every point. Had it not been for that premature paragraph contained in the first portion of the motion of the hon. member for Macleod, I would vote with them with my two hands. I entirely agree with them that the war debt should be paid by war taxes. I entirely agree with them that we should not diminish the war taxes as a whole, and that we should keep them before the eyes of our people as the price we have to pay for our criminal follies accumulated from 1914 to 1918. At the same time, I should not like to go too fast. I would not advocate paying off tod rapidly our debt, because if we want to preserve future generations from the calamity which a blinded public opinion, conducted by public men whose motives I will not qualify, but who sacrificed the present and the future interests of our country in order to serve foreign ends on another continent, I should like our descendants when the next war come3 to have something before their eyes that will cause them to say: Let us wait before we attempt to commit suicide once more.
