I think we should continue to bear a pretty heavy war debt and heavy war charges until the worlds atmosphere has cleared and until Canada has decided whether it belongs to itself or whether it is to be in the future, as in the past, the instrument of an imperialistic policy in the Pacific or the Atlantic, in Europe, Asia or elsewhere. Morley once said:	The
tax gatherer is a good school master. The present generation has listened to the lesson. Let the member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) endeavour to launch a crusade for an expedition to China, and he will find out that the present generation, in Ontario as elsewhere, has learned something of the lessons of the war. But twenty years hence? I do not know. Therefore until we have made up our minds what our duties are, what our national entity is composed of,' what our obligations are to ourselves or to somebody else-until that time I think it is a good object lesson for us to keep before ourselves a pretty stiff war debt.
But I think our war taxes, as all other taxes, need readjustment. I expressed that view last year; I still hold it. Something was done towards attaining that end last year. I am
The Budget-Mr. Bourassa

sorry to say that I do not find the same spirit in evidence this year. I do not think there was any necessity for the 10 per cent reduction in the income tax. It will give nothing to people with small means-they do not pay it-and very little to people who pay, let us say, $100 of income tax. The real beneficiaries will be the people with large fortunes and large incomes, that is, the people who are most responsible for the creation of that debt, and a large proportion of whom built up fortunes in the four years of war at the expense of our population-fortunes dipped in the blood of our sons. Instead of making that reduction, which will curtail the financial means of the government to meet our war charges, I think the government should have implemented the promise made last year by the late Minister of Customs, that if any change was made this year in the income tax it would be to exempt all children under 21 years of age and in charge of their parents. I repeat

it may be a hobby with me; I admit I am interested-we should always think of the family in these matters. We pretend to be one of the most advanced countries on earth, we pretend that our civilization, our literature, our system of education may stand on a par with those of the most enlightened countries. Well, what encouragement do we give fathers of families to endow their children with a complete education? We punish them for having children, we punish them for keeping their children at home in order to educate them. I say that is wrong, socially speaking. Better maintain the 10 per cent all round and make the fathers of large families benefit by the further exemption which was promised last year by a -then member of the government.
Now with regard to householders, they also have much to do with the family. Last year my friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) and myself joined hands with respect to this. I think we should put all householders on the same footing. At present the man who owns his house is exempt from taxation on its yearly value. An employee with moderate means who pays $500 or $600 rental is not allowed to deduct that as a charge against his income. I think we should all be put on the same footing, that there khould be a deduction, which could be calculated as a fair average, let us say, in cities of $500 a year, and in rural districts of $300 a year; and whether a man owns his house or pays rental he should be allowed to deduct that amount; but that if he owns a house worth $200,000 or $300,000 he should pay something

on the yearly value over and above what is necessary for providing the average class of habitation for a family. To show you the spirit, Sir, in which those things are considered, I was talking over that point last year with one of the highest officials of the department, a very honest and capable man. Here is what he put forward in objection to my proposition: "Well, that is pretty stiff. A man who owns a house worth $200,000 ought to be a useful citizen. I don't see why we should go for him." Surely if a business man, or a man with acquired or inherited wealth, has the means of living with his family in a house that has cost one-fifth of a million dollars, he is -capable of contributing a little more to the exchequer, of this country than the man who has to pay $40 a month to live in a rented house-with the danger of seeing his rental raised, as was done during the war by some of those people who pay nothing on the yearly value of their palaces -but doubled the rentals -of their tenants during the war-other patriots!
Let me mention a small matter, though I was told that it might be pretty important as far as the amount of money collected is concerned. I was given this information by someone closely connected with the making and operation of this income tax. I have seen myself in the American law and in the circulars issued by the American government to their various officials engaged in the application of the law, that the object of the' American income tax law is to tax all revenue at its source. With regard to the very large companies employing a considerable number of individuals you thereby reach the income not only of the companies themselves, but of all the individuals -connected therewith, in so far as these incomes are represented by salaries, profits, bonuses and so forth. On the other hand, I am told that the government, quite properly, has made arrangements with a number of foreign governments, the American, the British, the Belgian, I think, and several others to this effect: nationals of any of these countries living in Canada pay income tax in Canada only beyond and above the amount they would pay in their own country; and if our tax is lower they pay the difference to their own country. Canadian employees living in foreign countries and employed by Canadian companies do not fall into this category. The company deducts from its receipts all the salaries paid to the foreign employees, and these private incomes are not reached by the Minister of Finance. Their income tax is paid, for example, to the United States in the case of Canadians living

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
there. If we applied the principle which is in force across the border, we should reach the income at its source and in that way we might reap a pretty fair surplus of taxation.
With regard to the sales tax, I am not competent enough to offer any comments, not having had enough experience in that branch of taxation. I will say this, however. Last year I called the attention of the Minister of Customs to the situation of what I may call small rural industries, such as sawmills, sash, window and door factories, and so on. The minister informed me that he had already the power to exempt some of these and that he would secure the means of exempting others who had only a small trade. Let me give an illustration. There is, in my constituency-I am sure there are many similar cases elsewhere-a first rate labourer, a good intelligent fellow who grew up in his trade until he was able to put up a small plant which he operates with his son. Last year he brought me all his sales tax returns, the monthly sheets which he is obliged to fill up to meet the exigencies of the Customs department. In the whole year he had manufactured and sold no more than $2,200 worth of goods, out of which he had to purchase his raw material and keep a family of twelve; and he was exacted $110 in sales tax! Here is the father of a family of twelve paying $110 as his contribution towards the redemption of our war debt-for which I can assure you he was not responsible-out of a gross revenue of $2,200. Surely there is no sense in that. It may be asked, could he not have passed the tax on to the purchaser? Well, you know how it is in the country. Here is a very small factory and about a mile away there is a small mill where the individual gets his work done. The farmer, rather than pay the sales tax to the so-called manufacturer, purchases his lumber, goes to the mill, gets his work done there and so escapes the tax. Some consideration should be shown to such small traders.
I come now to the stamp tax, which has been called a nuisance tax. I fail to see that it is more of a nuisance to put a $10 stamp on a large cheque than a fwo-cent stamp on a small cheque, although I think it was a good thing to raise the margin from five to ten dollars. In my opinion, however, we could have required the use of stamps of denominations in keeping with the value of the cheques issued, without causing injury to anyone. I have already suggested, and I make the suggestion again, that there should be a stamp cheque on all coupons on debentures presented to the banks. I have been told by very well informed people that a large number
of our patriotic millionaires are evading the income tax through holding a large portion of debentures that are not inscribed, being anonymous and "payable to bearer." They do not declare these coupons and there is no possibility of the inspector ascertaining where they are. Dividends can be reached; the names of shareholders can foe discovered; but the names of bondholders cannot be got at. I suggest that a two-cent stamp on each coupon presented to a bank would not be much of a charge on debenture holders, and it would bring a comfortable revenue. That would be visible taxation; it would be equitable taxation; and it would be convenient and cheap taxation-cheap, that is, from the standpoint of the government. That brings in four of the principles of Adam Smith No. 1 and Adam Smith No. 2.
With regard to postage reduction, I voted last year for this measure, and while I cannot censure the government in this regard I think we were perhaps somewhat hasty. I do not want to compromise anyone, but I may say that I had an interesting conversation with a person in authority in the Post Office Department. I assure the minister at once that he was not criticising either the minister or the government, but he made the simple observation that had we kept that one-cent tax on letters we could practically have rural mail delivery all through Canada to-day, provided by the amount represented by the postage reduction. There, again, I think a 'little thought would have led to a more satisfactory outcome. It is true, as the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) observed, that the burden of that tax fell on large companies carrying on a heavy correspondence. Certainly the reduction means practically nothing to the farmer or to ithe labourer, being merely a matter of a few cents a year, and it would have been a substantial contribution to the improvement of the postal service, while being easy to bear.
I do not want to detain the House much longer, but in closing I desire to say a word or two regarding the redemption of the debt. His discussion of this question constituted the most interesting part of the speech delivered by the hon. member for West Calgary. It is this particular part of his address which I bear in mind when I say that the hon. gentleman, having qualified to lead the Tory imperialistic party as an advanced protectionist party, and having qualified further to resurrect the old Manchesterian Liberal party, apparently has qualified also for the leadership of socialism in offering what is perhaps the most advanced socialistic proposition I
The Budget-Mr. Bourassa

have so far heard in this House. Of course, I would not discard it on that account. I was reminded whole listening to the hon. gentleman of his propensity for quoting great Englishmen. Have you noticed, on political and parliamentary questions involving matters of precedent, how frequently the hon. gentleman resorts to Gladstone, while in economics Adam Smith seems to be his source of inspiration? I fancy a good Liberal conscience is haunting the powerful brain of the hon. gentleman. There I was reminded of an utterance of Sir William Vernon Harcourt when he was Chancellor of the Exchequer. One day he was introducing a measure, I forget just what it was, and someone interrupted saying: "That is socialism." He said: "What of that? Are we not all more or less socialists to-day?" In a sense -that is true. If by socialism we mean that we -must have regard to the interests of society, to the interests of the state, as covering and protecting the interests of the family and the individual, I am quite agreed on many socialistic ventures. No doubt society has been too frequently in the past sacrificed to individual interests and appetites or even grievances.
The plan proposed by -the hon. gentleman is interesting but it is just as well to see it as it is. He was interrogated three or four times by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Railways, I think: Well, is that not enforced borrowing? No, no, was the answer. Of course it is. I have worked in insurance companies; that is, I have endeavoured to create and to put on a pretty fair footing a small company in my province, and I know how this goes. The inspector comes every year, looks up the books of -the company, finds out what are the outstanding policies and what is the amount of the reserve. He comes there with the law in his hands and he tells the company: You must present me with a certain value of certain investments in order to respond to the requirements of the law. There is a list of investments that serves to cover the reserve. But if the state comes in and says:	The
first thing I do is to impose upon you 4 per cent national debentures which must form part of your reserve, then I say:	You force
the company to lend you money at 4 per cent. There is no use in playing with words.
I do not say it is wrong but it must be examined into carefully. In the case of large companies that have been operating for years I do not think there is any harm and, indeed, there may be much good in such a policy. But if you enforce upon small com-
TMr. Bourassa.]
panies at the beginning certain values and thus restrict their earning capacity, you may put them into a rather difficult position to start with. I admit however that is a detail that will have to be studied. What interests me is the advancing of -the idea and it has to be taken up. We must not start with the idea that some of those -things are repugnant to past traditions. We have broken all traditions. We have put upon the shoulders of the people of this country a war debt of $2,600,000,000 for a quarrel in which Canada was no more concerned than Greenland.

speechtext:
I have much less respect for those who -have -taken the best advantage possible of that sincere sentiment in some and of the imposition of that war burden upon the rest of the country, to enrich themselves. The sooner we reach them in the most practical manner the better. But unfortunately I am afraid that the further we get away from the war, -the more difficult that will be. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) that the honest, equitable and sensible manner in which we should have provided for the reimbursement of our war debt would have been a capital levy during and immediately after the war, would have been to follow up the growth of capitalism during the war, in order to find out the source of prosperity of many of the industries and individuals who gathered wealth during the war, while masses of the people were shedding their blood and paying out their money. But of course the further we get away from the war, the more difficult it will be to apply this principle of justice, because at the present time, with -the system in vogue not only in -this country -but all the world over, a vast proportion of that infernal wealth, acquired by theft and crime, by the exploitation of the good sense, the patriotism and the blood of the masses of the people, is in -the hands of other parties who are innocent of its origin. That is one of -the results of the system of modern capitalism. The creators of immoral,

The Budget-Mr. Cantley
unreal wealth, soon find means of getting so many people to partake of the titles upon which their wealth reposes, that they create a community, I will not say of accomplices, but of associates who cry out, " socialism,'" "communism" and "spoliation" the moment the state comes out and challenges the validity of their titles or endeavours to tax them. That is the great difficulty.
But at least let us see things as they are; let us confess the reality of things. Let us instruct the people on that very situation and by all means let us endeavour to readjust our fiscal policy. Let us try to impose the burden of taxation, I will not say so much against the rich as for the relief of the poor. I partake of the views of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) to this extent, that everybody must pay something, but I end with these words:	All
people must pay according to not only their means but their social usefulness to the nation and to the state. The father of a family who bears for twenty or twenty-five years the material and moral burden of raising the proper kind of children for this country is the best contributor to the material as well as to the moral wealth of that country, and I think that must be taken into account when you raise taxation and speak of the power of paying. The tax is not always paid in money although it takes a great deal of money to-day to raise a family. It is paid with mental effort, with moral dignity, with all contributions to the development of those young men and girls who will be the people of Canada to-morrow. I think everything we can do to help fathers of families to bear the social burden of taxation as easily as possible is the best contribution we can make to the prosperity of the country.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in continuing the debate on the budget I have no intention of tendering any lengthy or profuse compliments to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb); his native honesty is apparent to and his courtesy recognized by all members of the House irrespective of party affiliations. His ideals as to the best fiscal policy for this country naturally do not meet with the entire approval of hon. gentlemen on this side. Speaking for myself, I was disappointed, greatly disappointed, that the Minister of Finance made no provision looking to any relief or protection for the
iron and steel industry of Nova Scotia, or for any encouragement to the coal-mining industry of either eastern or western Canada. Providence has been exceptionally kind to the agricultural industry of this country during the past three years, and probably the great majority of hon. members will agree that whatever amount of prosperity we may have had in this country, be it great or small, is due almost entirely to the bountiful harvests which Canada has enjoyed during that period.
Before dealing with the budget I wish to refer to a statement made at the last session by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), and which is reported at page 550 of revised Hansard for 1926. Speaking on January 29th last year respecting our exports of raw materials, and replying to the then hon. member for South York, Mr. W. F. Maclean, he made some reference to the export of nickel from this country and its entry into Germany. The hon. member for Labelle had spoken of our extracting the mineral and sending it to the United States to be converted into the various forms for which nickel is adapted. Mr. Maclean interjected the remark "And to England", to which the hon. member for Labelle replied:
Not only to England, too, if my hon. friend will allow me. I should not like to open up that vista upon our so-called imperial policies, but I suppose my hon. friend knows that not a German warship could have been finished, not a German cannon could have been hardened to the point of usefulness, had it not been for the Canadian nickel controlled by the international company-
The hon. member for Labelle made some reference to the various armament firms of Great Britain, Germany and France, and then stated:
-so that every German cannon which was hardened with Canadian nickel and loaded with shells similarly hardened, which helped to kill sixty thousand of our sons, brought tremendous dividends to the numerous bishops, lords and members of parliament of England, who drew their dividends from the German weapons as well as the Germans did from English weapons.
These statements were commented on by the then leader of the opposition, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. Replying to him the member for Labelle again referred to the matter and stated:
I should not like to develop this theme at too great length now, as I hope to have occasion to do so at a later date. I may say, however, that all my information was secured in London from high officials of the Naval department, from gentlemen connected with the Department of the Chancellor of Exchequer and from people who have traced the capitalization of the armour trust under which all those companies drew their dividends.
The Budget-Mr. Cantley

consumed in the winter months after the close of navigation in the St. Lawrence, such an outlet would go far to furnish employment to our miners during this-under present conditions-season of unemployment.
I should like to point out further that, as to the reductions made in the agricultural implement duty and the relief afforded the automobile manufacturers last year, the great bulk of the cost of doing so fell on the iron and steel trade of this country, and largely on that of the maritime provinces. To illustrate that point I would like to -take one item as given in the returns, which shows that the importation of these items in 1924 reached a value of $2,211,000. In 1925 it was slightly less, $2,035,000, while for the year 1926 it rose to $3,463,287, an increase of more than fifty per cent. Owing to the provision that one-half the value of the automobile had to be manufactured in Canada our manufacturers of cars imported billets from abroad-chiefly from the United States, the balance' from Germany-and from such steel billets and bars forged the automobile axles. That provision did not help the steel industry of Canada one iota, because Canadian steel was not used in the production of automobiles; it was all imported.
The iron and steel trade has had to bear all, or nearly all, the reductions made in duties on agricultural implements. Under the tariff exceptions covered by items 445, 446, 446b, 447b, 448 and 591, the imports of steel from the United States in 1925 represented a value of $767,706; in 1926 that value had climbed to $2,037,000. But -that is not a fair statement of the case, because prior to 1925 this class of steel enjoyed a rebate of 99 per cent. Allowing for this, however, the fact remains that over $2,000,000 worth of steel was imported free from the United States last year for the making of -agricultural implements. The Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company at one time supplied a considerable proportion of the agricultural steel used by the implement makers of Ontario and Quebec, but due to putting practically on the free list most of the material used in the manufacture of agricultural implements, the Scotia Company have been forced to scrap fully a quarter of a million dollars' worth of plant, designed, built and installed solely for the purpose of producing steel for the manufacture of these implements. That capital has been lost and that portion of our trade wiped out. Therefore I say that the steel industry has had to bear the brunt of all the concessions given in recent years to both the implement and automobile manufacturers of this country.

The tariff board has functioned for about a year, and so far as the public is aware has accomplished very little of a constructive nature, and so far, as regards the coal or steel industries, simply nothing. The Minister of Finance this afternoon gave us more information than we have had hitherto in regard to what has been done by that board. I rather think that his statement of what it has achieved was not such as to greatly impress the House with its value.
I am sorry the minister is not in his seat, because I should like to point out to him what the situation is in some of the towns of the maritimes as a result of the condition of affairs that I have attempted -to describe. On the hillside above the Scotia plants at Trenton, also at New Glasgow, are hundreds of steel workers' houses. Many of them are empty; others are lost to the owners who, having invested the savings of a lifetime, are now being foreclosed and sold out by loan companies. The builders of these houses and hundreds of others of our best steel workers, mechanics and fitters, able to take their place alongside the best mechanics on the continent, are to-day in Detroit and other United States cities, solely because the steel trade of Nova Scotia has been -the victim of - a defective tariff policy.
I have before me a copy of the Canadian tariff. It contains about seventy items which are on the free list or under the 99 per cent rebate clause. This Canadian iron and steel tariff is the most irrational, illogical and mixed mass of oult-of-date items that it is possible to imagine. We have in this tariff items that have stood unchanged since the first iron and steel tariff was formulated in this country. Some of these items refer to classes of goods and materials that are not made and have not been -made -in Canada for twenty years.
I refer to Swedish rolled iron and rolled steel nail rods for horseshoe nails. No Swedish iron horseshoe nails have been made in Canada for years, and still that item remains as paint of the tariff. There is another item referring to the small spindle that goes into the knob of a door lock. It has stood on the free list for thirty yeaTS, although there is not a -mill in Canada that could not roll in a few shifts all of this material consumed in Canada in the past ten years. I could also refer the House to a lot of other items that are just as objectionable and just as ridiculous.
The iron and steel pipe makers of Ontario and Quebec are favoured by the present tariff to an extent that probably is not realized by many hon. members. They are able to import iron and steel skelp from the United States

The Budget-Mr. Cantley
or from any other foreign country ait a duty of five per cent, while they have a tariff on their own product running from 27i per cent to 30 per cent. There is no reason why the furnaces and mills of Nova Scotia generally should not provide that skelp, and would if we were given an equitable proportion of the protection on pipe. Surely, Sir, we are entitled to the same protection on steel skelp as the manufacturers enjoy on their pipe. I go further. We have a very much greater right to protection, because the capital employed in the production of the steel embraced in the skelp is infinitely greater than the capital employed in the manufacture of skelp inlto pipe. In addition to that, the volume of labour employed in turning skelp into pipe, which is a very simple operation, is very slight compared to the labour involved in the production of the skelp. Now, why should we have a tariff which discriminates against an industry in which large volumes of labour are employed and large amounts of capital are invested as compared with one in which the capital investment and the labour employed are trifling.
I should like to refer now very briefly to the question of coal. During the war years Nova Scotia bunkered the warships, battle cruisers, and converted liners, which kept the Atlantic trade route free to national and neutral commerce. With Nova Scotia coal was also bunkered thousands of British, allied and neutral steamers, liners and freighters, which put in for examination at both Sydney and Halifax en route to British and allied ports, being freighted with men, munitions and army supplies. Nova Scotia was then all-essential to the successful prosecution of the war. Now the war is over and our miners must remain idle during most of the winter months because of defective trade, tariff and transportation policies. To obtain the maximum output from our Nova Scotia collieries as now developed and equipped we must have more men during the active shipping season than are now available. At the present time, during the winter season, thousands are idle. This condition must be remedied and I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) and the government to now provide that remedy. This lack of men during -the shipping season will explain some of the difficulties to which our friends at the lower end of this side of the chamber have been referring in the last two or three days. It is imperative that we have more miners in the summer months in N ova Scotia than we have to-day if we are to attain our maximum output. What happens when the St. Lawrence is closed to navigation? We provided two and a half million
tons of coal for the St. Lawrence last summer.
It is indeed our only market. During the winter months that market is closed by ice. The result is that a considerable proportion of the miners in Cape Breton to-day are idle, including some of -those who recently came from the other side, although their condition is no worse than that of our native mining population. This condition is altogether due to the fact that we have not a sane, reasonable, workable tariff policy in regard to fuel. Why should we buy from sixteen to twenty million tons of coal a year from the United States when there lies in Canada, in the east, in the west and in the central provinces, one-seventh of the entire coal supply of the whole world? If we were sensible we would so regulate our affairs as to be independent as to fuel of any nation on the face of the globe. Why do we not do so? The time will come, and it will not be long deferred when the people of Ontario and Quebec will be unable to obtain American anthracite, which to-day they think indispensable. I have here some fifteen resolutions presented to the House of Representatives in the United States during the years from 1923 to 1926, memorializing congress to enact laws to prevent the exportation of anthracite to any country whatever. This for the reason that the people of the United States realize that within a very few years their supply of this coal will be entirely exhausted. I wish it were exhausted now, because there is no reason why we should buy one ton of anthracite coal from any source, especially when those who have it do not want to sell it to us.

This national fuel question is not a laughing matter; it is a serious question in the province of Nova Scotia and it, should 'be regarded in the same light by every member of this House, no matter from what section of the country he may come. I trust that the Minister of Finance when he comes to consider the Duncan report will so approach the question of coking plants that we shall be able to dispose satisfactorily of
The Budget-Mr. Cantley

our fuel problem, with a view to replacing American anthracite. If this were done it would not only be satisfactory to Nova Scotia but it would cheapen the cost of this form of fuel for the people of central Canada.
I have already made a slight reference to the tariff board and I want to offer the Minister of Finance a suggestion. The customs tariff as it now stands and has stood for several years is grossly unfair to the maritimes, and instead of a board of inquiry who, during a year's labour, have produced nothing tangible, the minister should himself investigate the matters affected, as did his predecessor, who took the trouble to go over the whole o.f Canada, holding sittings in various industrial centres and familiarizing himself with the actual conditions. He did not rely on any commission to supply him with information which he considered it his duty to obtain at first hand. The Minister of Finance is a level headed business Scot, and I hope he will appreciate the importance of the suggestion I make and act upon it. If he does we shall be delighted to see him in Nova Scotia, and to do what we can to give him all the information he wants which will be of benefit to him in his capacity of Finance minister as well as to the province of Nova Scotia and the Dominion at large.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Before I discuss the budget I desire to refer for a few moments to the address delivered by the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken). I was amazed at the extraordinary presumption of knowledge of farming displayed by that hon. gentleman, and the most astonishing statement he made in the course of his speech was that as a result of the introduction of certain improvements in farming implements, the farmers had nothing whatever to do between reaping and harvesting. That may be true in one or two instances where the farmers can grow their crops under dry conditions which enable them to use what is known as the combined harvester and so thresh as well as cut about the same time. But if the hon. gentleman knew anything at all about farming he would know that the number of these machines in Canada is quite limited, the cost being so very high; and he would know also that a good part of the price of these machines is due unquestionably to the protection which the implements still carry. Further on in his remarks, the hon. gentleman rebuked the farmers of the west, who he said were more prosperous than any other class of the population. I hope I quote him correctly. He

thought that the farmers in the prairie provinces were in a more prosperous condition than any other class, and he gave as the reason the fact that they received more privileges from governments than anybody else. He cited amongst other matters the Crowsnest agreement and pointed out that the country suffered because of the application of these rates, which were, he said, unfair. Further, that the railway companies did not profit by these rates; and so on. I do not wish to go at any length into a discussion of this question; I do not need to. The answer is clear and simple. Hon. members in all parts of the House who were members of the committee investigating the Crowsnest pass agreement, know very well that under oath before that committee the. unrefuted statement was made that even if the whole Crowsnest pass agreement were restored, rates under it, excepting in one instance, would still be higher than rates on the same commodities over similar distances in easterr Canada. That is my answer to the hon. gentleman who alleges that we are profiteering, so to speak, at the expense of the railway companies and also of the general population of this country.
Furthermore, quite recently Mr. Vien, a member of the Board of Railway Commissioners, made this statement to the Canadian Pacific railway counsel:
The Crowsnest rates are very, very profitable.
Subsequently Canadian Pacific officials under cross-examination agreed that the rates were very, very profitable. Where then does the argument of the hon. member for Toronto West Centre stand? The hon. gentleman should also remember this fact, that on all the products we ship from the western provinces outward for sale anywhere else we secure special rates only on export commodities. Our products when sold are sold subject to a deduction of transportation rates from the price. The hon. member should get into his mind this fact, that on the other hand manufacturers add to the price of their commodities the total freight to the destination, so that not only are we as primary producers compelled to have deducted from our price the transportation rates on what we sell at the time we sell it, but when we buy commodities from the hon. gentleman's friends in eastern Canada-and we are very glad when we can buy them; they are sometimes very

The Budget-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
good-we have to pay transportation charges upon them all the way out. We are thus caught both ways, and still he alleges that this is a special privilege to us.
There are many other questions which might be taken into consideration but I do not wish to dwell too long on the hon. member's speech. Let me take up briefly just one other point at this stage. He suggested that to-day, owing to the introduction of labour-saving devices, we were becoming very prosperous. Of course we know that is ridiculous. We know that the same labour-saving devices are applied in eastern Ontario and farming conditions there are anything but prosperous. Although in western Canada we had last year a relatively large crop, the grade was very low and the net result to the farmer was not high. On account of the quantity of grain reaped by most of us it was a year in which we did not lose as much as we lost in other years and some districts made gains. On the whole conditions were little better than those of t'he last five years so far as agriculture was concerned. It is only fair to make that statement. But for hon. gentlemen to suggest that we are amongst the prosperous classes is ridiculous.
About the time, let us say of Lincoln, out of every one hundred persons seventy were engaged in agriculture. This meant simply that seventy farmers or farming people produced enough food supplies for themselves and thirty others and, in addition, they may have had a little for export. To-day, as a .result undoubtedly of labour saving devices and improved farming methods, roughly thirty out of every one hundred persons are engaged in. agriculture. This means that thirty persons are supplying themselves and seventy others with food supplies and, in addition, have a vast surplus for sale in foreign markets. On that basis, if on no other, agriculture should be the most prosperous industry in this country, instead of being amongst the most depressed. The proposition is so simple that one need not worry about it any longer.
May I say to the Minister of Finance, a man for whom I have the deepest respect and affection, that he has succeeded at least in introducing into this House a rich man's budget. It is a triumph for the rich man in this country. It is disastrous for the poor man in this country. It offers nothing to the great working classes, the great masses of the people, except what they can secure on what may through good fortune be passed on to them through possible reductions in the price
of commodities as a result of the reduction in the sales tax. It is problematical whether retailers and wholesalers will .pass on that reduction except in the case of high-priced commodities; but as regards articles of low value there is very little possibility that any of the reductions will be passed on to the common people. Therefore let me sum the budget up at the opening of my remarks; let me give it a title, we will say. It is a rich man's budget. You will like Robb if you have a big income; you will not like Robb if you have not a big income. Some hon. members belonging to the august Conservative party to my right say that they do not like him; that they hate him. I think they do political^ speaking; none of us does, personally speaking.
The Minister of, Finance appears to have taken a good deal of his policies from Mr. Mellon. Mr. Mellon is a very astute man, but he represents, as no other man does in the United States, the big interests of that country. Far be it for me to say that the Minister of Finance represents the big interests of this country, but certainly he is doing his best to assist them. There have recently come to us some despatches in which it is indicated that Secretary Mellon's triumph in the enactment of the new tax law means that he has saved to the richest individuals and corporations in the United States more than $3,000,000,000 in federal taxes. We have not enough people in this country to enable the Minister of Finance to do that; but if we had, no doubt he would do it. Twenty millionaires were listed, showing the amounts they saved by the 1926 tax law over their tax of last year. For example, Mr. Rockefeller Junior, who gave $10,000 to the Republican ' campaign fund in 1924, saved, as a result of the introduction of that law, $2,762,000 of the payment of $6,277,669 he made in 1925. Mr. Henry Ford, who does not seem to have contributed to any campaign fund, is said to have saved $1,147,875, and Edsel Ford saved $949,544. Strangely enough, Mr. Mellon himself comes next-I do not know whether the Minister of Finance is in the same position; perhaps he can inform us later-with a saving of $828,348. He too gave $10,000 to the party campaign fund in 1924. Far be it from me to suggest that there is any connection between the income tax reductions of this year and the campaign funds of either party, but the time is now come in this country when the fullest possible examination into
634	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
the sources of campaign funds is overdue, and on that point I intend to dwell at some length a little later on.
Before I get to that stage let me take up the budget items in sequence. It is proposed to make a reduction of 10 per cent in all rates of the income tax. Last year's reduction was swallowed-well, reluctantly by some of the members of this comer of the House, because we were convinced, or had been convinced iby specious argument, that it meant an increase in taxation of the richer people and a saving to those who did not have big incomes. However, we unwillingly swallowed it. The situation in the House may have justified us to some extent in so doing. We had an extensive program of legislation to carry into effect, but notwithstanding the plausible argument that the rich were being taxed more and the poor less it would not have taken much for us to have opposed it. But this year no longer does there exist any excuse for supporting a budget which proposes to reduce the income tax all the way round. I say so because in this country the great majority of the people, by far the great majority of the people, pay no income tax, nor can they pay it. The income tax, indicated this afternoon, is a war tax. That is, it was introduced during the war years for the purpose of assisting in meeting the cost of the war. It was introduced into Great Biitain, about the time of the Grimean war for a similar purpose, but its advocates have always insisted on the introduction of the income tax in order that amongst other tax reforms it may be used by steadily increasing stages to replace unfair indirect taxation. Hon. members to the right of the Speaker, who are fairminded men who sincerely and conscientiously believe in low tariff and think that the future of this country depends upon the development of her natural resources rather than on the fostering of artificial industries, will certainly have some difficulty in explaining the position which they have taken so far on this point. They should not overlook the fact-I do not think they are overlooking the fact, they are simply blinding their minds temporarily to it; but it will foe brought subsequently to their attention with great force and strength that every step taken in the direction of reduction of income tax takes them further and further away from tariff reduction. Not only that, but it takes away from them the ability to tax those who can pay and are able to pay because of the war, because of the profits made in the war, because they were the 
people who accumulated during the war vast sums, vast fortunes, as a direct result of the war. It is true some of it has been distributed through death, inheritance, distribution of estates, and so forth, but the bald fact remains that the people who now *are in a better position than any others to pay income tax are those who have profited, either directly or indirectly, from war conditions. It is not fair to the public, it is not fair even to hon. members opposite, that a Minister of Finance should introduce into this House a budget in which I say to hon. members opposite they had no part. I challenge hon. members opposite to tell me if they were ever taken into consultation upon this budget. The public does not know it. The public assumes -always has assumed, I am sorry to say- that the Minister of Finance before the introduction of the budget at least consults the party that sits behind him and is supposed to support him. I do not believe a single member opposite saw the budget, had it read to them, or knew anything about it before it was brought into the House. They are in the position that I am. It is not until after its delivery that they are able to form any idea with respect to it or are in a position to criticise it. Is that fair? It is in my opinion a most ridiculous position in which to place hon. members. That the nation's annual statement should be prepared by one man without consultation with anybody else is bad enough, but .that he should budget for the nation's future, for the business or finances of the year, without consulting .any of his party other than possibly the Prime Minister, is a most ridiculous situation, and one which still further emphasizes the necessity for the private members in this House, on all sides and in all parties, to do what they can to strengthen their own hands, and to take away from the executive council the steadily increasing usurpation of the control of the House.
Now I am going to come to another stage in this discussion. The Minister of Finance in his budget statement indicated that the war depression had passed. There is not a man in the country believes that-.that is a man who thinks. There may be some who simply read headlines and will swallow such statements wholesale. There may be thousands in the country, aye millions, who, reading the headlines, "Twenty-seven million dollars tax reduction, twenty-seven million dollars savings to the people," will think that that is actually the case. It is so absurd to

The Budget-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
put the thing in that way that it would be hardly worth while answering if it were not for the fact that so many people will believe it. So will people believe that there has actually been a doing away with, a destruction of, post-war depression. There may have been some abatement, but if the Minister of Finance had only turned to the statistics he himself placed on Hansard without reading them to the House he would have seen that fifty per cent-no less than fifty per cent-of the annual expenditure is still directly attributable to the war. On page 390 of Hansard a table, placed there by the Minister of Finance, shows that interest on the public debt, the result of war, amounts to SI 16,607,000 and there are these other figures; war pensions, $36,650,000; soldiers' civil re-establishment, $7,200,000; soldier land settlement (administration), $1,300,000-and by the way it does not take into account the tremendous losses that are going to follow that unfortunate scheme; Imperial War Graves Commission, $810,000; battlefield memorials, $200,000; adjustment of war claims, $155,000; or a grand total of $162,922,000, directly attributable to the war. And yet the minister says that the war depression is over. Yet the minister says:	"Let us get rid of nuisance
taxes and war taxes." It is all right for my hon. friends to my right. They have always been supporters of indirect taxation and in opposition to direct taxation, but my hon. friends opposite have certainly nothing to be proud of in a budget of this type. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), who comes down here from Saskatchewan surrounded by a galaxy, a veritable squadron, of low-tariff men, now finds himself in the pitiable position of having to swallow a budget which has not a single tariff reduction in it but worse still represents action directly opposed to the whole principle of direct taxation and opposed to the very principles he himself has very frequently advocated. I admit that political exigencies may require him to adapt himself to conditions, but I cannot believe for a moment that the Minister of Railways is comfortable; even now he scratches his eyebrows with uneasiness and with worry.

One of the most eminent professors probably in this country, Dr. J. C. Hemmeon, of McGill university, recently gave a very illuminating and interesting address to a group of individuals in this city, and among other things said by him was this:
Income tax accounts for only eighteen to twenty per cent of the total federal taxation in Canada, while in the United States income taxation raises fifty per cent, and in Great Britain a still higher proportion.
Yet the Liberal government, Liberal with a large "L", is getting further and further away and collecting less than ever before from direct taxation. How under heaven is the party in power at the moment going to justify to the electorate, so badly deceived, the position they have taken on this question? The professor goes on:
It is a little strange that when our income tax was the same as the United States, they raised 30 times as much from this tax as we did in Canada.
Now wait for the question: Was not the population larger? Yes, but by how much? Twelve or thirteen times. There is the answer. I do not think we have had in Canada a more inefficiently conducted department than the department in charge of the collection of the income tax. My hon. friend from Toronto West Centre criticised the farming class to-day so bitterly on this question and charged that we were self-interested in our position with regard to the income tax, implying that the position we were taking as a group on this question was directed purely by self-interest, that we were not paying income tax as a class, and we -are not I admit except for a very small proportion. I do not think a more unfair statement could have been made. Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer a challenge to the government and to my hon. friend from Toronto West Centre. If the farmers are not paying income tax it is only because of one of three reasons, or a combination of them: (1) They have no income on which to pay the tax; (2) the income tax collectors are inefficient in collecting, are not looking after their job; or (31 the farmers are crooked and are deliberately defrauding the income tax collector.

It is with regret that I find the Liberal party adopting a policy of this kind.
On the question of farmers and the income tax, let me indicate to the hon. members for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr, Cahan) and Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) one of the reasons why the farmers have not paid income tax as a class generally. The total capital invested in agriculture in the year 1925, according to the Canada Year Book, was $7,508,645,000 The value of all agricultural produce in that year was $l,453,3oS,000. Note that the investment of $7,500,000,000 gave a return value on the produce raised of $1,453,000,000.
Now let us come to the capital invested in manufacturing. The amount is $3,380,000,000. The manufacturing production, less cost of raw material, was $1,311,000,000. In other words, with a total capitalization of a little more than twice as much, agriculture receives approximately the same amount of return as the manufacturers do. Is it not a ridiculous position for a manufacturer to rise and claim for one instant that the farmers are defraud-

The Budget-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
ing the country in regard to the income tax, that they are evading it, getting rid of it, and dodging it, While they,-the manufacturers- have placed upon their shoulders the full burden of it? You cannot convince the farmer that that is the case.
Now I come to one other question. For the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1926, the excise tax collected on matches, a pretty useful little article, was $3,991,999. On the basis of these collections the reduction the income tax made by the Minister of Finance this year will amount to roughly $548,000, over half a million dollars. Now, let us see who is going to get it. In the pre-war years if you went into a store you could buy one of these small boxe3 of smoker's matches for a cent. Taxation was imposed and the price went up to two boxes for five cents. These two boxes carry half a cent excise duty apiece, the two together one cent. The minister cuts off 25 per cent of that one cent-one-quarter of a cent. I ask any hon. gentleman in this House to indicate to me how the retailer is going to pass on to you or to me as consumers that quarter of a cent saving. So much for that. The housewife goes into a Dominion store and buys three boxes of matches in a single carton costing 25 cents, each box holding 300 matches, or 900 in all. The total saving on that carton as a result of the tax reduction will amount to 21 cents. Who is going to pass that on to the consumer? The fact is clear, Mr. Speaker, that not one cent of that $580,000 will go back to the consuming public; but it is a direct loss in revenue to the country. Who get it? Well, I hesitate to suggest that the hon. member for West Calgary Mr. Bennett) will benefit in any degree from it. It might enhance the value of his stock-but that is his own business anyhow. The fact of the matter is that the match companies in this country will have to pay to the government $5S0,O0O less this year than they did last year, supposing the consumption of matches is relatively the same. They may pass the saving back to the wholesaler, 'being very honest and altruistic.
They must.

All right, we will grant that they must. The wholesaler might pass it back to the retailer. But the hon. gentleman who has just interrupted me, the Minister of Railways, himself knows that as far as the western part of this country is concerned we do not deal in fractions of five cents. He knows that all over western Canada you would be laughed at to suggest that you

Far be it from me, Sir, to suggest that this is the result of any peculiar situation that may have developed, but it is significant to note that there appears to have been established during this session an understanding of some nature or other in which the public certainly are interested, and upon which the public should be informed-an understanding between both the old parties.

Well, perhaps my hon. friend had better wait a moment before he becomes too voluble about it. I read with considerable interest, after indeed listening to it previously, the speech of the hon. member for West Calgary. The whole tone was so placatory, so mild, so unlike the usual form of criticism that we have had in so able a manner from Sir Henry Drayton and other financial critics in past days, that one at least suspected there might be an ethiopian dodging around somewhere in this old woodpile. I was not surprised then at the speech by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) delivered some time previously, and I began to understand it. It was an amazing speech for a member of this House who has in the past been one of the bitterest critics the party opposite ever had, and one of the most able, a man who prepares himself with the greatest care, but tinctures with the bitterest gall the criticism he pours on members opposite.
He may have seen the error of his ways.

He may
have, but one wonders, and is justified in wondering, what sudden and extremely illuminating light came upon him to show him the error of his ways. It might have been a match-it might have been the striking of a whole box of matches. I thank the hon. member-I am not sure what constituency he comes from-for the suggestion, coming as it did from my hon. friend's own party. In his speech the member for Vancouver Centre intimated that the Conservative party had

This afternoon we advanced several important bills for the Minister of Finance with scarcely any comment,-

-and I must say that the ministry have been very prompt in making brief statements and explanations.

I am exceedingly anxious that we should expedite the business of this session. We have had a couple of years of pretty hard parliamentary duty, and I think both the country and parliament will be the better for a little surcease from bitterness and controversy.
